title: Nested Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
one_liner: To predict future traffic at each intersection, first predict what the whole city will do, then use that big-picture forecast to guide predictions for each neighborhood.
lead: Traffic forecasts are hard because cities are complicated: what happens at one intersection depends on many neighbors, and patterns change over time. Most methods try to predict everything at once, which gets confused. This paper proposes thinking in layers: first predict big regional trends, then use those trends to steer precise predictions for each individual spot.

problem.h2: Predicting traffic is like guessing a crowd
paras: Traffic at each intersection next hour depends on: weather, nearby roads, time of day, and how traffic flowing from neighbors affects flow here. The naive approach tries to predict all 500 intersections independently, or all at once using one giant equation. Both fail under real-world noise.

With independent predictions, you miss that neighborhoods move together. With one-giant-equation, the model gets overwhelmed by high-frequency jitter and loses the big trends. It gets stuck trying to memorize random spikes instead of learning that Tuesday afternoons have a predictable pattern city-wide.

callout.html: Models trained to predict every intersection fine-grained traffic fail to capture how large regions move together, and they get drowned in local noise.

steps.text: Use affinity (how similar each pair is) to group nearby intersections into M regions using spectral clustering.
Run two separate neural networks: one reads 12-step history for each intersection, one for each region.
The region encoder outputs a coarse forecast (the big picture 12 steps ahead).
Let each intersection query the region forecast, pulling its own prediction toward the regional trend.
During training, mask some future regional guidance and rebuild it, teaching the model to cope when guidance is missing at test time.

paras: The paper changes how future information flows into predictions. Normally, a model predicts each intersection independently. Here, the model explicitly constructs a coarse future forecast at the region level, then channels that forecast down to each intersection prediction via attention (a learned weighted average). The intersection predictions are no longer solo; they are pulled by the bigger picture.
object.object: Future macro forecast, injected via attention

hidden.name: Regional coherence score
paras: Regional coherence measures how much each intersection's prediction aligns with its region's trend. High coherence means the intersection prediction has incorporated the regional pattern. The paper estimates this by attention weights (learned scales): when an intersection piece (or representation) pays strong attention to its region's piece, coherence is high.

The paper uses this implicitly in the cross-attention mechanism. At training, intersections that attend (pay attention, or weight the input heavily) more to the regional signal improve more. During rollout (multi-step prediction), intersections with higher coherence to their region are more stable because they are anchored to a larger, smoother signal.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger attention to regional signal. Highlighted intersections pull more from the region's trend.

reads.html: Imagine a radio broadcast of the city's overall traffic direction. Intersections that listen closely to that broadcast make steadier predictions than those ignoring it.

Cross-attention weights (learned scales showing how much to listen to each signal) between node pieces and regional pieces quantify how much each node incorporates the macro guidance. High weights correlate with lower error during multi-step rollout (step-by-step generation where predictions feed back as input).

mechanism.h2: Why it works: Hierarchical constraint and stable rollout
paras: Spatio-temporal forecasting is hard because noise at each intersection masks the large pattern. Without guidance, the model overfits to jitter. By forcing the model to also predict regions (coarse scale), the model learns that big patterns are smooth and repeatable. When it then steers each intersection prediction via cross-attention to the regional forecast, each intersection's prediction is anchored to a signal it knows is true (it just predicted the region). This anchor prevents the model from chasing noise.

During multi-step rollout (generating 12 steps by feeding your own predictions back as input), errors compound: each wrong step feeds into the next, amplifying drift. But if intersections attend to regional predictions, and regions change slowly, the region forecast stays stable longer. Even if an intersection prediction drifts slightly, the regional signal pulls it back. The multi-step rollout with masked guidance during training teaches the model to trust and repair the regional signal even when pieces are missing, so it learns to hold onto that signal tightly across all prediction steps.

stages.s: 12 historical steps per intersection and per region
Predict regional coarse forecast and node-level candidates
Cross-attention: let each node attend to its region
Blend node candidate with regional pull via attention weights
Final 12-step forecast per intersection, informed by region

math.words: For each node i in chunk k, compute its representation as the average of its historical values in that chunk. Then measure how similar each pair of nodes is using distance, converted into affinity by an exponential: nodes that are close in history have high affinity.
symbols: Affinity score between node i and node j (0 to 1, higher means more similar)
Historical time series of node i during chunk k
Bandwidth control (how sharply affinity drops with distance)
Euclidean distance (straight-line distance between time patterns)

worked.title: A tiny worked example with 3 intersections
lines: Intersection A and B: historical distance in chunk 1 is 0.5, in chunk 2 is 0.4. Average squared distance = (0.5^2 + 0.4^2)/2 = (0.25 + 0.16)/2 = 0.205.
With sigma=1, exponent = -0.205/2 = -0.1025. Affinity A_AB = exp(-0.1025) = 0.903 (very similar).
Intersection A and C: average squared distance is 2.5. Exponent = -2.5/2 = -1.25. Affinity A_AC = exp(-1.25) = 0.287 (not very similar).
Spectral clustering groups A and B together into region 1, C into a different region, because their affinity is high.

math.note: High affinity pairs end up in the same region, so the region forecast captures correlated behavior.

bars.h2: What improves when regions guide nodes

charts.title: Baseline (node-only forecasting)
charts.note: Errors grow as the model chains predictions forward; no regional anchor.

charts.title: With nested forecasting (region + node)
charts.note: Regional guidance stabilizes long-range predictions; errors shrink by 25% at step 12.

items.b: Spectral clustering may miss real boundaries
items.html: If the affinity matrix (built from historical similarity) does not match true spatial structure, regions become artificial. For example, two geographically distant intersections that happen to have similar traffic patterns might be grouped together, ignoring actual road topology. The region forecast then predicts correlated noise rather than true regional motion.

items.b: Rollout error accumulates when the region forecast drifts
items.html: During multi-step rollout (12 steps ahead), if the region's prediction is slightly wrong at step 5, that wrong input flows into step 6 and beyond. The node predictions are anchored to bad guidance. The masked guidance reconstruction loss helps reduce this drift because it teaches the model to recover from partial missing guidance, training it to be less sensitive to small errors, but it cannot fully prevent all drift because real forecasts at far horizons have irreducible uncertainty.

During training, the region forecast is given (teacher forcing). At test time (when the model runs on new data), it must be generated from its own predictions (rollout). Without the boundary masking strategy (randomly dropping regional guidance during training), the model overfits to perfect guidance and fails when running on real data.

items.b: Done right: regional guidance is stable under noise
items.html: The method works when regions aggregate nodes with similar periodic patterns. Traffic patterns repeat weekly; spectral clustering on historical data usually captures these repetitions. Regional predictions are smoother than node predictions because they average across many nodes, so they resist jitter. Node predictions anchored to smooth guidance are naturally more stable.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny spatio-temporal forecasting task: a grid of 25 intersections in a 5x5 lattice, with 5 regions defined by spatial proximity. Generate 1000 steps of synthetic traffic: each intersection has a 100-step periodic pattern, plus Gaussian noise. Train a baseline model (node-only attention) and the nested model (regional encoder plus cross-attention). For each model, forecast 12 steps ahead using autoregressive rollout (feeding predictions back as input). Compare mean absolute error (MAE) on held-out test data.
demo.metric_eq: Stability gap = (baseline MAE at step 12) minus (nested MAE at step 12). Positive means nested forecasting is steadier over long horizons.
demo.closing: The demo must show that as rollout steps increase, the baseline error grows faster than the nested model's error, proving that the regional guidance keeps predictions from drifting because the guidance provides a stable anchor that resists accumulated noise, whereas the baseline has no such reference point and errors snowball.
